The activity view: every connection, the rule it matched, and where it went. What is Rouler? Rouler is split tunnelling for Windows. You choose which network interface each app uses: a privacy VPN for your browser, a work tunnel for work apps, and your normal connection for everything else. They all run at the same time. It does one job at the network layer, sending each app's traffic out the interface you chose. It isn't a VPN or a firewall. Rouler works with network interfaces, so it isn't tied to a particular VPN. Use the official WireGuard client, Tailscale, Mullvad, OpenVPN or AmneziaWG, and run several side by side. If Windows has an interface for it, Rouler can send traffic over it. A rule can match an app, a destination IP or subnet, or both. So one app can use different interfaces for different destinations. Your VPN clients keep running as they normally do, and there's nothing to import. Rouler uses its own Windows network driver, written in Rust. It's small and fast, and it changes as little of your system's networking as it can. Make rules for programs and for Windows services, so background services use the interface you choose instead of your default one. Rules for packaged apps and folders are coming. A live view shows every connection, the rule it matched, and whether it was diverted, routed by Windows, or blocked. No digging through logs. Detailed control over each app's traffic, in an interface that stays out of your way. A few of the screens you'll use. Pick the interface Point a rule at a specific interface, or let the system route it. Scope by IP range Narrow a rule to an IP range. Rouler shows which interfaces can reach it. Rule from any connection Right-click a connection in the activity view to make a rule from it. Why it works the way it does Like a lot of people, I can't stand software that sits in the background interfering with everything: Discord overlays, junk utilities for a monitor or mouse, motherboard software that tries to install a copy of Norton. It never ends. So Rouler is built on a few rules: No system hooks, no virtual network adapters, no user-mode proxy, no custom NAT, and nothing that trips game anti-cheat. Rouler builds on what already ships in Windows. Every action Rouler takes shows up in the app. If it did something, you can see it. It should be quick and stay out of the way. Rouler only touches traffic you've written a rule for. A rule matches an app, optionally narrowed to a destination IP or subnet, and sends it out the interface you pick. Anything without a rule goes through normal Windows routing. For example, take a machine with three interfaces: So these rules all work together: Chrome's other traffic has no rule, so like Steam, Windows routes it as normal. Rouler applies a rule just before Windows makes its routing decision, and leaves everything else alone. Rouler doesn't edit your route table. Each interface's routes still decide what it can reach, so you can run as many interfaces as you like, as long as their routes don't conflict. In everyday use, you won't notice Rouler is running. Games and calls feel the same with Rouler on. The delay it adds is too small to measure. Uploads run at full speed, even on a 2.5 Gb/s connection, and downloads are never slowed. Rouler uses very little CPU in normal use. It only works hard under loads far beyond what real apps send. The installer is just 4.3 MB. Minimised to the system tray, Rouler settles to about 15 MB to 20 MB of memory within 30 seconds. For the full results, or to run the same tests on your own PCs, see the Performance doc.
